subject: Agriculture
title: Selective Breeding of Livestock
description: A fast breakdown of Selective Breeding of Livestock for builders.

hook.text: Robert Bakewell looked at scrawny English sheep and asked: what if I only bred the biggest ones?

buildup.text: In the 1760s, Bakewell kept detailed records, mating only animals with desirable traits.

discovery.text: Within a generation, his New Leicester sheep were twice the weight of typical sheep.

twist.text: Bakewell's methods worked so well that average cattle weight at London markets doubled by 1800.

climax.text: Selective breeding revolutionized livestock. The same principles later inspired Darwin's theory of evolution.

punchline.text: Better breeding fed a nation—and inspired a theory.

quiz.question: Who pioneered systematic selective breeding of livestock in the 1760s?

details.summary: Selective breeding of livestock transformed scrawny wild-descended animals into the productive breeds we know today. This topic covers Robert Bakewell's pioneering methods, the rise of breed registries, and how selection reshaped cattle, sheep, and pigs over centuries.
details.whyItMatters: Selective breeding turned livestock into efficient food producers. Bakewell's 18th-century methods doubled sheep and cattle weights within generations, providing the protein that fueled industrializing nations.
takeaways: Robert Bakewell pioneered selective livestock breeding in 18th-century England
Average sheep weight doubled within a century through systematic selection
Breed registries and studbooks formalized breeding goals and maintained pedigrees

faq.question: How did Robert Bakewell revolutionize livestock breeding?
faq.answer: Bakewell selected and mated animals with desirable traits—fast growth, more meat, better wool—rather than breeding randomly. He kept detailed records, practiced inbreeding to fix traits, and rented his improved bulls and rams to other farmers.

faq.question: What impact did selective breeding have on livestock productivity?
faq.answer: Average cattle and sheep weights roughly doubled between 1700 and 1850. Modern dairy cows produce 10 times the milk of their ancestors. Chickens reach market weight in 6 weeks compared to 16 weeks in the 1950s.
